'''''Sporobolus montevidensis''''' is a species of [[Poaceae|grass]] known by the common name '''denseflower cordgrass'''.<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SPDE2|taxon=Spartina densiflora|accessdate=24 November 2015}}</ref> Although reclassified after a taxonomic revision in 2014,<ref>Peterson, PM, et al (2014) A molecular phylogeny and new subgeneric classification of Sporobolus (Poaceae: Chloridoideae: Sporobolinae), Taxon 63: 1212-1243.</ref> it may still be referred to as '''''Spartina densiflora''''' by some users. It is native to the coastline of southern South America, where it is a resident of [[salt marsh]]es. It is also known on the west coast of the North America and parts of the [[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean coast]] as an [[introduced species]] and in some areas a [[noxious weed]]. In [[California]] it is a troublesome [[invasive species]] of marshes in [[San Francisco Bay]] and in [[Humboldt Bay]], where it was introduced during the 19th century from Chile in [[Ballast tank|ballast]].<ref name=spartina>[http://www.spartina.org/species/spartina-densiflora_v2.pdf ''Spartina densiflora'' field guide, Invasive Spartina Project]</ref>

==Description==
This perennial grass generally lacks [[rhizome]]s. It grows in erect clumps of slender stems that can reach 1.5 meters tall. The long, narrow, gray-green leaves are rolled inward, especially when new. The [[inflorescence]] is a narrow, dense, spike-like stick of branches appressed together, the unit reaching up to 30 centimetres long. The flowers are colorless and the spikelets are tipped with bristles.

==Invasive species==
This species has negative impacts on the salt marsh habitat of the California coast. It forms tight clumps of herbage that raise the elevation of the plants in the marsh, keeping the water from flowing in as far as it naturally would, and increasing [[sediment]] accumulation.<ref name=spartina/> It competes with its native relative, [[California cordgrass]] (''Sporobolus foliosus''), and other marsh plants such as [[Salicornia|pickleweed]] (''Salicornia pacifica'').<ref name=spartina/> Efforts to eradicate ''Sporobolus montevidensis'' and related hybrids in the San Francisco Bay area reduced the coverage to approximately 41 square meters in 2014, down from about {{convert|1.7|ha|acre|abbr=off}} in 2005.<ref>http://www.spartina.org/documents/2014ProgressReport_wCover.pdf, 2014 ISP Monitoring and Treatment Report, August 2015. Accessed 7/12/18.</ref> However, it continues to expand in the Humboldt Bay region.
